chief_complaint: sudden sharp left lower tummy cramps followed by passing bright red blood
hpi_details: Presents with acute onset of cramping left lower quadrant abdominal pain that began 4 hours ago after a mild episode of lightheadedness. Two hours later, passed an urgent bowel movement consisting almost entirely of maroon-coloured liquid and bright red blood mixed with small stool fragments. Pain partially eased after the bloody movement, but left lower quadrant tenderness remains.
ideas: thinks a blood vessel ruptured inside her colon due to hardened arteries
concerns: worried she might lose too much blood and require major bowel surgery or a blood transfusion
expectations: wants blood tests, IV fluids, and a colon scan to confirm where the bleeding came from
pmh: peripheral arterial disease, coronary artery disease post-stenting 5 years ago, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease stage 3
medications: clopidogrel 75mg OD, atorvastatin 40mg OD, ramipril 5mg OD, metformin 500mg OD
social_hx: ex-smoker 35 pack-years, lives with husband, retired school principal

investigation_events.title: Urgent ischemic colitis results
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent laboratory and CT results are now available; hydration, bowel rest, and serial abdominal examinations should not be delayed.

results.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
results.value: Segmental circumferential wall thickening and submucosal edema from the splenic flexure through the descending colon with reduced enhancement; no pneumatosis or free air

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Ischaemic Colitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Most cases of ischaemic colitis are transient and non-gangrenous: manage conservatively with IV crystalloid hydration, bowel rest (clear fluids initially), and optimization of cardiac output and blood pressure, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden sharp left lower tummy cramps followed by passing bright red blood

Key HPI features: Presents with acute onset of cramping left lower quadrant abdominal pain that began 4 hours ago after a mild episode of lightheadedness. Two hours later, passed an urgent bowel movement consisting almost entirely of maroon-coloured liquid and bright red blood mixed with small stool fragments. Pain partially eased after the bloody movement, but left lower quadrant tenderness remains.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: check for tachycardia or hypotension. Abdominal exam: localized tenderness in LLQ over the descending/sigmoid colon, no peritoneal signs. Bloods: FBC, urea/creatinine (baseline CKD check), coagulation profile, lactate. Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy (shows segmental erythema, oedema, petechiae, or cyanotic mucosa typically in watershed areas: splenic flexure or rectosigmoid junction). CT abdomen with IV contrast.
Relevant background/PMH: peripheral arterial disease, coronary artery disease post-stenting 5 years ago, type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease stage 3
Current medications: clopidogrel 75mg OD, atorvastatin 40mg OD, ramipril 5mg OD, metformin 500mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Ischaemic Colitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute diverticular bleed without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Vascular risk factors (peripheral arterial disease, prior stenting) with acute pain and bleeding — raises concern for bowel ischaemia.
management_principles: Most cases of ischaemic colitis are transient and non-gangrenous: manage conservatively with IV crystalloid hydration, bowel rest (clear fluids initially), and optimization of cardiac output and blood pressure
Monitor serial lactates and abdominal exams for signs of transmural infarction requiring surgical resection
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 73F with vascular risk factors presents with acute onset of cramping left lower quadrant abdominal pain that began 4 hours ago after a mild episode of lightheadedness. Two hours later, passed an urgent bowel movement consisting almost entirely of maroon-coloured liquid and bright red blood mixed with small stool fragments. Pain partially eased after the bloody movement, but left lower quadrant tenderness remains.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: check for tachycardia or hypotension. Abdominal exam: localized tenderness in LLQ over the descending/sigmoid colon, no peritoneal signs. Bloods: FBC, urea/creatinine (baseline CKD check), coagulation profile, lactate. Flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy (shows segmental erythema, oedema, petechiae, or cyanotic mucosa typically in watershed areas: splenic flexure or rectosigmoid junction). CT abdomen with IV contrast.
reference_soap.assessment: Ischaemic colitis (non-occlusive colonic ischaemia affecting watershed zone). DDx: acute diverticular bleed, infectious colitis (E. coli O157, Campylobacter), inflammatory bowel disease flare, colon cancer.
reference_soap.plan: Most cases of ischaemic colitis are transient and non-gangrenous: manage conservatively with IV crystalloid hydration, bowel rest (clear fluids initially), and optimization of cardiac output and blood pressure. Avoid vasoconstrictive drugs. Monitor serial lactates and abdominal exams for signs of transmural infarction requiring surgical resection. Flexible sigmoidoscopy within 48 hours for confirmation.

learning_objectives: Distinguish colonic ischaemia (crampy LLQ pain followed by bloody diarrhoea) from acute mesenteric arterial occlusion (diffuse agonizing pain out of proportion to exam)
Identify anatomical 'watershed areas' (splenic flexure and rectosigmoid junction) vulnerable to hypoperfusion in vascular patients
Formulate a conservative supportive management plan for non-gangrenous ischaemic colitis while monitoring for surgical emergencies
Evaluate antiplatelet and antihypertensive medication balance during an acute gastrointestinal bleeding presentation

teaching.one_liner: Reduced blood flow to a watershed area of the colon injures its lining, causing sudden crampy left-sided pain followed by passage of bloody, maroon-coloured stool.
red_flags: Vascular risk factors (peripheral arterial disease, prior stenting) with acute pain and bleeding — raises concern for bowel ischaemia

must_ask.say: Did the cramping come first, and the bleeding follow a couple of hours later?
What colour was the blood — bright red, or more maroon and mixed with the stool?
Do you have any circulation problems, or have you had a heart stent placed?
Did you feel lightheaded or dizzy just before this started?
Did the pain ease off once you passed the blood?
Do you have diabetes, and did you used to smoke?

history.answer: Doctor, I suddenly had terrible cramping pain in the lower left side of my tummy, and a couple of hours later I passed a lot of dark red blood into the toilet.
It was mostly a dark maroon liquid mixed with bright red blood and tiny flecks of stool.
It came out all mixed together with liquid bowel movement into the toilet bowl, not just a drop on the toilet paper.
It happened once about two hours ago, filling the bottom of the toilet bowl, maybe about a cup of bloody fluid.
No, there was no sharp or tearing pain around my back passage when the stool passed.
No, I have never felt any lumps, hemorrhoids, or itching down there.
No, I have never had trouble with constipation or had to strain to go.
My bowels have always been once every morning until this sudden episode today, and I haven't noticed my stools getting thin.
The pain came on suddenly four hours ago as severe sharp cramps in my left lower belly, about a seven out of ten.
I passed loose watery stool with blood, but I haven't had any mucus, fever, or chills.
Just before the stomach cramps started four hours ago, I felt a wave of dizziness and lightheadedness, but no racing heartbeat or fainting.
No, my weight has been steady and I haven't felt unusually tired before today.
No, I haven't had any pain in my upper stomach, heartburn, nausea, or vomiting of blood.
I do not have any liver problems, hepatitis, or history of heavy drinking.
I take a daily blood thinner called clopidogrel, but I don't take aspirin, ibuprofen, or iron pills.
No, I haven't eaten any beets, blueberries, or blood sausage recently.
I had a screening colonoscopy four years ago that was completely clear, and nobody in my family has ever had bowel cancer.
The sharp cramps in my lower left belly started first four hours ago, and then the bloody bowel movement followed about two hours after that.
Passing that bloody bowel movement took away the sharp cramping feeling, but a dull tender ache is still sitting in my left lower side.
I have poor circulation in both of my legs, and five years ago I had a heart stent put in for blocked heart arteries.
I have peripheral arterial disease, coronary artery disease with a stent five years ago, type 2 diabetes, and mild chronic kidney disease.
I had a stent placed in my heart five years ago, but I have never had any stomach or bowel operations.
I take clopidogrel 75 milligrams, atorvastatin 40 milligrams, ramipril 5 milligrams, and metformin 500 milligrams, all once a day.
I don't have any known allergies to medicines.
I used to smoke a pack a day for thirty-five years, but I quit completely five years ago after my heart stent.
I don't drink alcohol at all.
I am a retired school principal and I live at home with my husband.
My father had high blood pressure and passed away from a stroke, but there is no family history of bowel disease or cancer.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, pulse is 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, temperature is 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.
Blood pressure decreases slightly by 6 mmHg and heart rate increases by 10 beats per minute upon standing, with no symptomatic lightheadedness.
Mild conjunctival pallor is present bilaterally; sclerae are non-icteric.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no scars, distension, or visible pulsations.
Bowel sounds are hyperactive throughout all four quadrants.
Moderate localized tenderness is elicited on palpation in the left lower quadrant over the descending colon, with no palpable mass or rigidity.
No rebound tenderness or abdominal guarding is elicited.

No external anal fissure, hemorrhoid, or skin tag is seen; digital rectal exam reveals normal sphincter tone, no palpable rectal mass, and the examining glove shows maroon-stained liquid stool with a trace of bright red blood.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are bilaterally diminished to 1+, while femoral and carotid pulses are normal.
